Abstract

A photograph of a machined part already contains its dimensions. Reading them out means running a renderer backwards: finding the CAD parameters whose image matches the photograph, and knowing how sure we are. That makes a renderer a measuring instrument, and an instrument has to be exact before it can be precise. We describe irys, an open-source Rust renderer built to that standard.

Its differentiable core is path replay backpropagation on a GPU wavefront. Materials are written once as graphs in the tang tensor compiler and lowered both to GPU kernels and to an f64 CPU reference. An integer random-number generator, fixed-order reductions and a ray-only BVH walk make the replay reproduce the forward pass bit for bit: 65536 of 65536 lanes, with gradients identical across runs. GPU f32 gradients agree with the f64 reference to . On top of the material gradient sit pose gradients through instanced CAD meshes (primary edges, an interior term with attached frames, and secondary edges that move shadows and reflections) and a per-vertex image gradient that the vcad BRep kernel pulls back to the dimensions of a part.

Each layer is a measurement. A robot arm read from its CAD source gives back three joint angles and its anodised finish from a render, to 0.07° and 0.005. A bearing bore’s diameter gets its image gradient through the BRep kernel, matching vcad’s forward mode to . We state the instrument’s limits alongside its readings: replay is bit-exact per device and driver, the pose fit converges only near the answer, and recovering whole CAD programs from photographs is the subject of a companion paper.

1 Introduction

To measure a part, you usually touch it: calipers, a coordinate-measuring machine, a gauge pin. A photograph touches nothing, yet it already contains the part’s dimensions, mixed up with its pose, its finish, the light in the room and the lens. Separating them is inverse rendering: find the parameters whose rendering matches the photograph. For an engineered object those parameters are not free-form vertices or a neural field. They are the dimensions in a CAD model, the angles of a mechanism’s joints and the finish of its surfaces. If a renderer can recover them, and say how well it knows each one, it is a measuring instrument.

An instrument has two obligations. It must be exact: the same input gives the same reading, and the reading means what it says. And it must be precise: its error is small and known. For a differentiable renderer, exactness is a property of the gradient. Path replay backpropagation 1 made physically based differentiable rendering practical by replacing the stored path tape with a second, replayed pass. That only works if the replay regenerates exactly the paths the forward pass drew; otherwise the gradient belongs to a different estimator from the one rendered. Systems built on general array compilers 2 meet this contract inside one process and one backend. We wanted a GPU tier and an f64 CPU reference that run the same material source and agree to rounding, with each tier bit-identical across runs. Then a failing gradient test is a bug, never noise, and a reading can be trusted.

This paper describes irys, the renderer behind vcad and our robotics tools, and how it meets both obligations. Its contributions are:

  • One BSDF source, two lowerings, two tiers. Materials are tang tensor graphs. tang lowers each one to an evaluation program and an adjoint program, emitting WGSL kernels for the GPU and running the same graph in its f64 interpreter for the CPU reference. The path logic (ray generation, traversal, bounce, accumulation) is hand-written (Section 3).
  • PRB on a deterministic wavefront with hero wavelengths and NEE. The estimator is Vicini et al.‘s with next-event estimation, as in Mitsuba 3; what is new is a wavefront whose replay is bit-identical, with four wavelengths per path and the light-sampled lanes folded into the same graph batch (Section 4).
  • Bit-exact replay by construction. An integer RNG that is exact on both tiers, fixed-order reductions with no float atomics, and a BVH walk that depends only on the ray (Section 5).
  • Pose gradients through instanced CAD meshes. Primary edge sampling with crease ownership and visibility-aware importance, an interior term by forward-mode duals with attached frames, and secondary edge sampling for moving shadows and reflections (Section 6).
  • Validation at every layer and a fit on a real robot. Gradients against central differences with common random numbers, GPU against CPU f64, and a joint pose and finish recovery on an arm read from its CAD source (Section 7).
  • A bridge to CAD parameters. A per-vertex image gradient that the vcad BRep kernel pulls back to the dimensions of the part, shared as a benchmark with the companion paper 3 (Section 7.5).

1.1 Scope and limits

  • Determinism is per device and driver. The GPU tier runs in f32, so its results agree with the f64 reference to rounding, not bitwise; it is bit-identical against itself on one device and driver.
  • Materials. The differentiable material is a GGX conductor with a three-band spectral Fresnel. Diffuse surfaces and the environment are not differentiated. Gaussian splats are rendered but not differentiated.
  • Lights. The environment is the only emitter (a sky and a von Mises–Fisher sun lobe).
  • Pose parameters are rigid. Joint angles and the camera move instances rigidly. Non-rigid shape change enters only through the BRep bridge of Section 7.5.
  • The pose fit has a basin. The elbow converges from within about ±5° of the answer and fails from outside it; the blur and pyramid schedules we tried did not widen it reliably.
  • Hardware. All timings come from one Apple M-series machine through Metal; the exact chip was not recorded in the source logs, and timings in this draft are not yet regenerated on a single pinned machine (Section 9).

2 Background and related work

Differentiable path tracing. Li et al. introduced edge sampling to account for visibility discontinuities in Monte Carlo rendering 4. Radiative backpropagation 5 and path replay backpropagation 1 reduced the memory of the adjoint pass to a constant per path; Dr.Jit provides a tracing compiler for such methods 2. Visibility can also be handled by reparameterisation 6, by warped-area sampling 7, or by projective sampling 8; we compared warped estimators for the secondary term and chose edge sampling (Section 6).

Spectral rendering. Hero wavelength sampling 9 traces several wavelengths along one path, the hero choosing directions. We use it unchanged and make each wavelength its own PRB lane.

Compilers for rendering. SLANG.D adds automatic differentiation to a shading language 10 and is the closest analogue to writing BSDFs as tang graphs. Laine et al. argue for splitting a path tracer into wavefront kernels 11, the structure we use.

Differentiable rendering systems. Mitsuba 3 12 implements path replay with next-event estimation and multiple importance sampling, projective sampling and reparameterisation on Dr.Jit, and is the closest system to irys’s differentiable core. irys differs in what it guarantees rather than in the estimator: a replay that is bit-identical to the forward pass by construction, an f64 reference that runs the same material source, spectral transport with hero wavelengths, and visibility terms adapted to CAD tessellations (coplanar slivers, crease ownership, attached frames).

Inverse CAD and measurement from images. Recovering an editable CAD description from observations is usually posed as program synthesis over meshes, point clouds or drawings 13–15, and close-range photogrammetry measures manufactured parts by triangulating targets and features 16. irys supplies what both lack for photographs: exact gradients of a rendered image with respect to a part’s pose, finish and dimensions. CAD parameters upstream of the mesh are differentiated by our companion paper’s BRep kernel 3, joined to irys in Section 7.5.

3 Materials as compiled graphs

The differentiable material has parameters : GGX roughness with height-correlated Smith masking, and a Schlick Fresnel whose is interpolated between three spectral hats. It is written once as a tang TensorGraph whose inputs are per-lane columns (the cosines at a vertex and the hero wavelength’s hat weights) and whose is broadcast. tang lowers it two ways. The eval program returns and its pdf. The adjoint program is the backward pass of , so the batch sum over lanes is the reduction to . Each program is emitted as WGSL, one kernel per materialised comprehension, or as compiled C in f32 and an interpreter in f64 for the CPU. The interpreter matches a hand-written f64 GGX to , and the compiled C matches the interpreter to in the worst relative error.

The path logic is hand-written, in WGSL for the GPU and in Rust for the CPU reference: ray generation, BVH traversal, bounce, the throughput update, the final splat and accumulation, and the device-side loss scoring. tang’s comprehensions are straight-line bodies over fixed shapes, so data-dependent path loops and a traversal stack cannot be expressed in them today. Sampling the GGX visible normals is detached, since it needs no derivative under PRB, and the divisor pdf is the sampler’s, which we test against the graph’s pdf to .

4 Path replay on a wavefront

Estimator. For a path with vertices and radiance , BSDF-only PRB accumulates at each vertex, where is the radiance collected before vertex . With next-event estimation and multiple importance sampling the gradient becomes

where is the BSDF-sampled direction, the light-sampled one, the NEE contribution at and the radiance up to and including it. The MIS weights are functions of detached pdfs and therefore constants under . In the wavefront the light-sampled lanes are the second half of one graph batch, so a single adjoint dispatch serves both strategies. A nonlinear loss needs the primal image before the adjoint, so the loss is scored between the forward and replay passes; seeding the adjoint from the same pass instead biased roughness from 0.6 to 1.0 in our first spike.

Hero wavelengths. Each path carries four stratified wavelengths, the hero and its rotations by of the visible range 9. Only the hero draws directions. The wavefront’s lanes are (path, wavelength) pairs, four times as many as paths, and each lane is its own PRB path. At equal paths, four wavelengths cut per-pixel variance 7.4× in total and 28.7× in chroma.

Memory. PRB stores nothing per vertex. With four wavelengths a path costs 63.1 f64 words at depth 2 and at depth 8 alike. Memory scales with paths, not pixels. Frames larger than one dispatch are traced in chunks, and a 1024² image at 4 spp, 16777216 lanes, replays bit-identically in nine chunks.

5 Determinism

PRB’s replay must redraw the forward pass’s paths. irys makes this hold in four ways.

  • Same pipelines. Forward and replay dispatch the same compute pipelines over the same bind groups; they differ only in a uniform that enables the store of .
  • An integer RNG on both tiers. SplitMix64 is ported onto pairs of 32-bit words built from 16-bit limbs, so the GPU, which lacks 64-bit integers, produces exactly the CPU’s stream. A uniform keeps the top 24 of 53 bits, so both tiers walk the same paths up to f32 rounding of the geometry.
  • No float atomics. The reduction over lanes is tang’s monoid reduction, split 256 ways with one workgroup per parameter and a fixed combining tree. Splat accumulation runs in bounce order, loss scoring uses a fixed stride and tree, chunks are summed in order, and the device prefix sum used by edge sampling has a fixed order.
  • A walk that depends only on the ray. BVH traversal uses a fixed-size stack, visits the near child first by slab entry with a deterministic tie-break, and culls by the closest hit so far. The walk, and therefore the floating-point sequence, is a function of the ray alone, not of thread scheduling.

The result is that the replay reproduces the forward radiance bit for bit on every lane, 65536 of 65536 at depths 2 and 8, with NEE, and through the two-level instanced scenes and a garden scene of meshes and Gaussian splats; two runs give bitwise-identical loss and . The guarantee holds per device and driver. A different GPU or compiler may round differently, and then agrees with the CPU reference only to f32 precision.

6 Pose gradients through instanced CAD

Scenes. A scene is a two-level BVH: one bottom-level tree per CAD part or group, and a top-level tree over instances, each with an object-to-world transform. irys maps rays into an instance’s space without renormalising them, so hit distances compare across instances. A pose , such as joint angles, is a map from parameters to the transforms of the moving instances. The full robot in this paper has 2.4 million triangles, tessellated by vcad from its CAD source (a text format of parametric solids).

Primary edges. Moving an instance moves the curves across which the radiance arriving at the camera plane jumps: silhouettes, boundaries and creases between faces that are not coplanar. By Reynolds transport, a pixel’s derivative includes

over the projected edges , where is the edge’s outward normal and the normal speed of the material point under 4. We sample edges with density proportional to screen length times an importance (1 for silhouettes, a dihedral weight for creases, a small weight for back-facing edges), trace the two sides pixels apart with common random numbers, and require the inner ray to hit the edge’s own triangle or a coplanar neighbour. CAD tessellations are full of slivers thinner than , and without that coplanar rule the estimator loses most silhouette samples. A crease between two front faces is owned by the face that meets the eye more squarely, so its jump is counted exactly once. A low-resolution buffer of which instance each pixel sees lets the sampler demote edges it shows hidden, which cut variance 1.9× at equal samples. Sampling runs on the device, with a fixed-order prefix sum; it took the edge term on the arm from 105 ms to 7.4 ms per iteration.

Interior term and attached frames. Away from discontinuities the estimator is smooth in at fixed random numbers, and we differentiate it by forward-mode dual numbers through a re-trace of the frame: ray–triangle intersection with the corners as duals, the shading frame, GGX sampling and evaluation, NEE and the MIS weights. The renderer builds a vertex’s tangent frame from its normal with a construction that flips sign when the normal crosses a plane, a discontinuity in at fixed random numbers that no edge term sees. We instead differentiate the estimator whose frame on a moving instance is rigidly attached, . At it is the rendered estimator exactly, and for every it is an equally valid estimator of the same image, so its derivative is an unbiased estimate of from the paths the forward pass already drew. The duals reproduce the forward pass’s values to .

Secondary edges. When an instance moves, its shadow and its reflection move too. We sample the edges seen from each path vertex with a per-tree edge BVH, under one-sample multiple importance over three densities: geometric, toward the sun’s cone, and toward the mirror lobe. The boundary term includes the velocity of the BSDF-sampled direction, obtained by inverting the sampler at the path’s random numbers and redrawing it in duals. Against warped-area estimators on the same configurations, edge sampling had 14–19× lower variance at 1.6× lower cost.

Camera. The same machinery differentiates a seven-parameter camera (translation, rotation, field of view), with the eye, axes and field of view as duals and every instance’s edges as candidates.

7 Results

Unless stated, we check gradients against central differences (CD) of the same estimator with common random numbers; “frozen” means the random numbers are fixed so the CD is noise-free. Monte Carlo comparisons report a z-score, the difference over its standard error. Timings are release builds on the M-series machine above. The number in each table is read from data/measured.tsv, whose rows give the source test and commit.

7.1 Correctness of the material gradient

7.2 Variance and throughput

At equal samples per pixel, NEE with MIS lowers per-pixel variance 4.5× against BSDF sampling alone on a scene of two instanced boxes, with image means agreeing within noise. A gradient of the 96×96, 8 spp frame at depth 4 (73728 paths, four wavelengths each) costs 7.5 ms on the GPU without NEE and 14.9 ms with it; the forward pass alone takes 0.87 ms, about 85 million paths per second. The same gradient through the compiled-C CPU tier costs 116–129 ms, so the GPU tier is about 15× faster end to end. Most of the gradient’s time is the replay, because the adjoint’s four-parameter reduction is not yet fused and NEE doubles the batch.

7.3 Pose gradients

On a box against the sky, where the edge term is the whole derivative, edge sampling matches CD within 3.3, 0.8 and 1.3 standard errors on its three pose parameters, and the device’s f32 edge term matches the CPU’s f64 to . On the shaded arm over a floor, the edge and interior terms alone miss CD by z = 3.8, −3.9, 3.4: the arm’s shadow on the floor carries about 15% of the gradient. With secondary edges the same check gives z = 0.77, −1.07, 0.06.

7.4 Joint pose and finish recovery on a robot arm

The target is the arm at shoulder pitch, shoulder roll and elbow (−25.78, 16.04, −60.16)° with a bead-blasted clear-anodised finish . From (−8.6, 3.4, −37.2)° and a default finish, Adam on the image MSE for 600 iterations reaches (−25.73, 16.07, −60.23)°, an error of at most 0.07°, and , within 0.005 of the truth. The final MSE, , equals that of the true parameters re-rendered with fresh noise (), so the fit has converged to the noise floor. An iteration costs 112 ms for the material gradient on the GPU, 167 ms for the primary edge term and 66 ms for the interior and secondary terms on the CPU; the run takes 244 s. This is one run. We have not measured convergence over seeds or starting points, and starts outside the elbow’s ±5° basin fail.

7.5 From pixels to CAD parameters

The edge sampler’s velocity is a projection of the material point’s motion, so replacing the pose’s velocity with a unit translation per axis yields for every mesh vertex. vcad’s differentiable seam 3 takes exactly that cotangent on the nodes of a frozen tessellation and returns the derivative with respect to a CAD parameter in one reverse pass. The shared benchmark uses rose’s left shoulder-pitch output plate, a 3 mm rounded plate with a 49 mm bearing bore and twelve bolt holes, with the bore diameter. irys renders vcad’s frozen tessellation, the mesh whose connectivity the kernel holds fixed while it differentiates node positions (4942 nodes, 9932 triangles) as it is, against the sky at 160×128, under a fixed smooth image loss.

A finite difference that rebuilds the part is not a usable reference here. Rebuilding at loses node correspondence for mm and changes topology at mm, where the bore rim’s segment count, chosen from the circle’s size, drops by one; below that the render difference is quadrature noise. The pullback has no step size. It is exact for the frozen mesh, and irys’s sampling error is the only noise in the result.

8 Discussion

Why insist on bit-exact replay. With an exact replay, a gradient that disagrees with its reference is a bug in the estimator, not an artefact of the replay. We could therefore set every gate in this paper tight and debug failures by bisection. That is how we found the crease-ownership bug in our first edge sampler. It inflated one parameter’s edge term by a factor of five on a shaded arm while the mask-only test passed.

The f64 reference. Running the same tang graph in f64 on the CPU separates three error sources that are otherwise entangled: estimator bias (CPU against frozen CD), device rounding (GPU against CPU), and Monte Carlo noise (live sampler against CD over seeds).

Future work: from photographs to CAD programs. The readings in this paper fit parameters of a model we already have. The harder reading is the model itself: given a few photographs of a part, find the editable CAD program, its features and their dimensions, with error bars. irys’s gradients make the dimensions tractable inside such a search, and a printed tag fixes the camera and the scale. What remains open is topology: which features the part has. We take that up in a companion paper 17, with a held-out evaluation and a continuous relaxation over a program’s optional features.

Remaining gaps. The secondary term runs on the CPU in f64 and costs about a quarter of an iteration; its estimate is heavy-tailed, and the rose check passes at 64 seeds but not at 256. The device edge sampler is biased low on the robot by a few percent for a cause we have not found, so the fits use host samples. The adjoint’s reduction is not fused. Splats are not differentiated, and only the environment emits light. The elbow’s narrow basin limits the fit to starts near the answer.

9 Reproducibility

irys is open source under Apache-2.0. Each row of data/measured.tsv names the test or example in crates/irys-diff that measures it and the commit that introduced it; the rose-arm fit and the BRep benchmark need the rose CAD checkout. This draft’s rows are collected from irys’s design log at the commits listed. They were measured on different days, and every timing quoted is a release build. Before submission they will be regenerated in one pass on one recorded machine by a script in paper/irys/repro, as for the companion paper.

10 Conclusion

Seeing becomes measuring when the renderer that explains a photograph is exact and its gradients can be trusted. irys makes the gradient exact where it can be: a replay that reproduces the forward pass bit for bit, materials compiled from one graph to a GPU tier and an f64 reference, and pose and shape gradients through the instanced CAD a kernel produces, down to the dimensions in the model. With them, a robot’s joints and finish read back from its render, and a bore’s diameter gets a gradient from its pixels. The next reading is the CAD program itself, from photographs of a real part. irys is open source.
